title: Taiwan’s Status Is Ambiguous. U.S. Policy Shouldn’t Be.

Taiwan’s Status Is Ambiguous. U.S. Policy Shouldn’t Be.

It’s time for the U.S. to embrace strategic clarity.

By David Raikow, a political advisor specializing in armed conflict and a former U.N. diplomat in Sudan, South Sudan, Libya, and Afghanistan.

For generations, significant elements of international policy have turned on a concerted global effort to ignore an obvious truth: that Taiwan’s legal status is ambiguous. Beijing is adamant that it is sovereign over the island. Taipei is adamant that it is not. Domestic political pressures prevent either from allowing any appearance of giving any ground. Neither is able to unilaterally impose its view on the other; even a “successful” invasion of Taiwan would devastate China’s economy and quite possibly break its military, while a Taiwanese declaration of independence would almost certainly prompt Beijing to demolish the entire island despite the costs and risks.
Most of the rest of the world has sought to accommodate both maximalist positions at the same time, largely by formally accepting Beijing’s view while de facto adopting Taipei’s. By focusing on public rhetoric rather than underlying interests and actions, unfortunately, these efforts ultimately produced decades of miscommunication, uncertainty, and dangerous crises.

Beijing is adamant that it is sovereign over the island. Taipei is adamant that it is not. Domestic political pressures prevent either from allowing any appearance of giving any ground. Neither is able to unilaterally impose its view on the other; even a “successful” invasion of Taiwan would devastate China’s economy and quite possibly break its military, while a Taiwanese declaration of independence would almost certainly prompt Beijing to demolish the entire island despite the costs and risks.
Most of the rest of the world has sought to accommodate both maximalist positions at the same time, largely by formally accepting Beijing’s view while de facto adopting Taipei’s. By focusing on public rhetoric rather than underlying interests and actions, unfortunately, these efforts ultimately produced decades of miscommunication, uncertainty, and dangerous crises.
The public U.S. position on this point is particularly tangled, opaque, and in many specifics self-contradictory. Administration after administration has twisted itself into pretzels attempting to maintain “strategic ambiguity,” grounded in former President Richard Nixon’s 1972 statement that the U.S. “acknowledges” and “does not challenge” Beijing’s position on Taiwan without endorsing or adopting it. Congress has since repeatedly attempted to distance this U.S. “One China policy” from Beijing’s “One China principle.”
The resulting mess has left both Beijing and Taipei to fill in the gaps while contending with domestic political pressures and real concerns about worst-case scenarios. U.S. President Donald Trump further muddied the water in the immediate aftermath of his May trip to China by casting doubt on long-standing U.S. commitments to Taiwan.
This approach serves no one, least of all Taipei or Beijing. The United States is in a unique position to remove much of the volatility from the Taiwan Strait by making a clean break from strategic ambiguity and openly embracing key realities of the current political environment.
First, Taiwan’s status is, in fact, ambiguous. While that ambiguity is at times awkward, it has for generations allowed all involved nation-states to maintain peaceful relations while serving the interests of their people.
Second, the only viable means to resolve this is by an entirely peaceful and voluntary agreement between Taipei and Beijing. Any attempt to do so unilaterally or by the use of force, coercion, or intimidation will inexorably lead to a globally catastrophic war. Until Taipei and Beijing can reach such an agreement, the status quo will remain the best option available for everyone.
Third, the United States’ top priority must be to avert war by dissuading both Beijing and Taipei from any attempt to resolve this question unilaterally. This should include a firm and explicit commitment to help Taipei defend itself against any use of force, intimidation, or economic coercion. It should also include explicit and affirmative efforts to discourage any unilateral Taiwanese action that risks war.
Fourth, the U.S. should disavow any position at all on the questions of Taiwanese sovereignty and of how many Chinas there might be. These are matters to be determined by agreement between Taipei and Beijing. As long as such an agreement is made in the absence of any use or threat of force or coercion, it is not the United States’ place to attempt to dictate its terms.
The status quo in the Taiwan Strait is far more stable than U.S. observers often portray it. It’s true that absorbing Taiwan with its economy and infrastructure intact and functional would be a huge victory for China on the international stage, and likely an even bigger one for whichever Chinese leaders could take credit. That outcome, however, is simply not on the table.
There is no plausible scenario in which China can “win” an invasion of Taiwan any time in the foreseeable future. Invading an island is incredibly difficult, even for a capable and overwhelmingly superior force. The People’s Liberation Army (PLA), while large and well-resourced, is also inexperienced and untested. As of 2026, no active PLA officer or unit has fought in a shooting war, and a series of purges has left significant gaps in its chain of command. Much of its advanced weaponry and equipment—including items that would be critical to any amphibious assault—has also never seen actual combat. Under these circumstances, the Republic of China Armed Forces might be able to repel a PLA landing even without U.S. intervention.

A successful PLA landing, on the other hand, could prove even more painful to China than a failed one. Any outcome in that case would include the destruction of most or all of Taiwan’s infrastructure, including most definitely the crown jewels of its economy: its semiconductor foundries. Given their overwhelming dominance in the field and the difficulty of replacing them, this would almost certainly send the entire global economy into a disastrous tailspin, taking China along with it.
The status quo, meanwhile, offers China significant access to the Taiwanese and broader global economies, a strong international position, and a manageable domestic political environment. This is the best China’s leadership can reasonably hope for under the circumstances, and it seems well aware of this.
While Beijing’s posturing is often aggressive, it is almost exclusively focused on managing intense political pressures at home while deterring a formal declaration of independence from Taipei.
These responses have largely been limited to messaging and symbolic moves that, while sometimes risky and provocative, have stopped short of direct intervention. Even the current Taiwanese position that the island is already an independent state has prompted a relatively muted response from Beijing—a tacit acknowledgment that this does not cross the same red line that a formal declaration of independence undoubtedly would.
By the same token, neither Taiwan’s current government nor its people appear to consider the status quo ideal. In each of the last three presidential elections, the Taiwanese electorate has chosen vocally pro-independence candidates by substantial margins. In a June 2026 National Chengchi University poll, only 7.6 percent of Taiwanese respondents wanted either rapid or eventual unification with China, and only 34.4 percent wanted the status quo to continue indefinitely.
The risks of any further move toward independence, however, are huge. Chinese President Xi Jinping has done his utmost to signal that he is unwilling to be seen as the leader who “loses” Taiwan, and that he is willing to destroy Taiwan to prevent that outcome. He faces extreme domestic political pressure on this issue; Chinese public sentiment regarding Taiwan is intense, deeply rooted, and bolstered by lifetimes of government propaganda. While capturing the island intact is beyond the PLA’s capacity, laying it waste is not.
For Taipei, the status quo offers almost all of the material benefits of independence at relatively low risk, and again both its people and its political leadership seem to recognize it as the best available option. The ideological and cultural interests in full and formal independence are important to many, as are the hope for more certainty and an end to the looming threat from the mainland, but large majorities of the population seem to accept the trade-offs involved.
In the 2026 Chengchi University poll, 87.9 percent of respondents saw the status quo as the best option for the present, while only 4.5 percent favored “independence as soon as possible”. Much as Xi has used aggressive posturing to manage domestic political pressures, Taiwanese presidents Lai Ching-te and Tsai Ing-wen have attempted to push pro-independence rhetoric just up to Xi’s red line without crossing it. Even their current public line that Taiwan is already independent is carefully calibrated to position them as defenders of the status quo. The Taiwanese electorate, for its part, has favored the opposition party in midterm local elections, in part to discourage Lai and Tsai from taking independence talk too far.
As with both Taipei and Beijing, U.S. administrations have long seen the status quo as imperfect but far superior to any realistic alternative. Washington, however, has considerably more political room to openly acknowledge this, and by doing so mitigate the pressures that threaten the stability the other two both prefer.
Beijing will respond with loud and aggressive public messaging, but not actual aggression. Chinese public opinion will demand a performative rejecting of the end of the One China policy, while Chinese leadership is likely to understand that it can gain far more from a clear recognition of its red lines and a U.S. commitment to steer well clear of them. Taipei may object to a more overt U.S. position against independence but gain far more from clear and firm U.S. military and economic defense commitments. Both will benefit from a de-linking of U.S. defense support from independence rhetoric. Relationships between all three will benefit from the U.S. formally removing itself from any discussion of what an eventual resolution should be, so long as Taipei and Beijing arrive at it peacefully and voluntarily.
Ambiguity and clarity are both important tools in international law and diplomacy. Ambiguity is often necessary for agreements, flexibility, and adaptation to new conditions. Clarity builds trust, stability, and effective crisis response. As with most important tools, it is often crucial to understand when and how to use one rather than the other. If U.S. ambiguity was ever the best tool in Taiwan policy, that time has long passed.

David Raikow is a political advisor specializing in armed conflict, systemic corruption, and political simulation design. He previously served as a U.N. diplomat in Sudan, South Sudan, Libya, and Afghanistan.
